participation.text: Government institutions included examination-based recruitment for some educated men; this is not universal access.

evidence.text: A tomb figure preserves an elite representational context rather than a named person’s complete life.

coordination.text: Neighborhood gates, government recruitment and religious translation organize different kinds of work; their rules do not establish universal access or compliance.

name: Tang China: a capital and its many connections
geographicPrecision: Capital locator; no claim that one city represents all Tang society.

interval.label: Tang dynastic frame, 618–907 CE
interval.note: Conventional dynasty dates; individual objects and political disruptions have their own chronology.

question: What does a tomb figure reveal about the living city?
summary: Chang’an joined court government, neighborhoods, markets and religious communities. People moved through a built environment that organized access as well as exchange. A tomb musician presents one carefully made image of courtly life; it cannot stand for the city’s whole population. The capital and its institutions changed within the Tang dynasty’s long conventional frame.

sections.title: An inherited capital needed people to make it work
sections.text: The Tang did not begin with an empty landscape. A new capital had been built under the preceding Sui, south of the earlier Han city. Rulers inherited government institutions as well as streets and buildings. Offices needed people who could read and write; the examination system offered some educated men a route into service. Access still depended on education and social position. A recruitment procedure describes one way of staffing government, rather than demonstrating that every resident could participate equally.

citations.locator: Sui rebuilding and distinct earlier Han site

sections.title: Walls and gates shaped an ordinary errand
sections.text: The NUS seminar summary describes walled residential wards, gates, markets and a curfew that restricted movement. Going out for supplies therefore depended on more than distance: opening times and permission mattered. The diagram separates a ward, a public street and a market as functional settings. It gives no surveyed route or uniform house plan. The summary explicitly calls reconstructed ward interiors conjectural; their residents did not all occupy identical compounds.

citations.locator: One-page summary, ward/curfew and reconstruction paragraphs

sections.title: A musician is an image made for a tomb
sections.text: The earthenware figure holds an implement with ribbons or strings which the Met compares with castanets. Pigment and shaped clothing give the figure a specific visual character. Its catalogue classification is tomb pottery. Someone selected, made and placed an image of performance for a funerary setting; this is different evidence from a performer’s own testimony. The sculpture supplies neither a personal name nor a record of wages. Its seventh–eighth-century date is narrower than the whole Tang frame.

sections.title: Religious communities and government changed together
sections.text: Xuanzang returned to the capital in 645 with texts that he subsequently translated. The university account distinguishes the pagoda first built in 652 from rebuilding in 701–704. Translation and storage required sustained institutional work, beyond the moment of arrival. Different religious communities lived in the capital, but their presence did not guarantee permanent security. Persecutions in 845 and the dynasty’s continuation after a major mid-eighth-century rebellion prevent a single timeless picture of openness or stable court authority.

citations.locator: Final paragraph: continuing dynasty after rebellion

claims.text: The dynasty continued after the mid-eighth-century rebellion, despite weakened court authority.
claims.checkedBy: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval

returnPrompt: What would you need to learn about people who could not afford such a burial?

deeperReading.title: A reconstruction can test a question without filling every gap
deeperReading.text: A regular grid does not reveal who lived behind each wall. The NUS summary distinguishes evidence about wards from conjectures about their interiors. Its example of Bai Juyi’s compound belongs to Luoyang; it is not a measured house in Chang’an. Use the diagram to ask how gates organized access, then seek dated records of actual movement. Geometry alone cannot show that every rule was obeyed.

citations.locator: One-page summary, Bai Juyi and conjectural reconstruction

deeperReading.title: A city’s surviving buildings run on different clocks
deeperReading.text: The university essay carries the reader from the Han and Sui capitals to Tang religious buildings and later Ming structures. This makes a practical method: identify which phase a surviving feature belongs to before using it to picture a whole city. A building first founded in one year can contain substantial later rebuilding. Similarly, a tomb object can illuminate representation without locating its original workshop or the household of a living performer. Comparing these sources requires several dated histories, not one illustration labeled “Tang life.”

citations.locator: Successive capitals and later surviving structures

deeperReading.title: Two kinds of learning served different tasks
deeperReading.text: Compare recruiting an officeholder with translating returned scriptures. The first selects people for government service; the second makes a body of writing available through another language. Both require learned work, but sharing a capital does not make their audiences, purposes or opportunities identical. The tomb musician adds another form of skilled activity represented in the city’s wider courtly culture. Ask who could enter each setting and whose own voice survives. The comparison broadens institutional history beyond a ruler’s list of achievements.

evidenceReading.title: Read a plan, an object and a dated account differently
evidenceReading.introduction: These are source paraphrases and modern teaching interpretations, not translated ancient regulations.

items.label: Walled wards in a seminar summary
items.text: Heng’s seminar summary describes gates and curfew; reconstruction of interiors remains conjectural.
items.interpretation: A spatial rule helps explain constrained movement. It does not supply the pictured musician’s address.

items.label: A catalogue classifies a figure
items.text: Met 1978.345 is seventh–eighth-century tomb pottery with pigment and a percussion-like implement.
items.interpretation: Catalogue identification and visible features support a funerary representation of performance, not a personal biography.

items.label: A building was rebuilt
items.text: The pagoda’s first foundation and its early-eighth-century rebuilding are separate in Waugh’s account.
items.interpretation: A founding date does not date all standing fabric. A modern photograph needs the same care.

familyActivity.title: Plan an errand through a gate
steps: Find the ward, gate, street and market in the supplied diagram.
Trace an imagined daytime errand with a finger. Which opening must the person pass?
Close that gate with a finger. Explain what additional information would be needed before saying the errand could still happen.
familyActivity.explanation: The diagram is a modern functional guide. It helps ask about access and timing; it does not reconstruct a named resident’s actual trip.

review.reviewer: Codex source consultation and self-review; not independent historian approval
review.scope: Bounded C5 account with main/deeper/evidence reading, family entry, phased context, sourced geography and modern explanatory media.
limitations: No original Tang legal-code or household-register consultation; the ward source is a one-page seminar summary, not the full study.
No surveyed city/ward reconstruction, named musician biography or renewed verification of every Tang event.
Wider rural society, taxation, military households, women’s lived experiences and late-Tang transformations need further research.

placeStudy.title: Chang’an and Luoyang: keep the city examples distinct
placeStudy.description: Approximate modern city-area locators orient two settings in the sources. The Chang’an point is not a precise outline of either the Han or Sui/Tang city. The diagram’s ward is conceptual and is not plotted as an excavated neighborhood.

points.label: Chang’an / Xi’an — capital area
points.text: Waugh distinguishes the earlier Han city from the Sui rebuilding and Tang capital. This city-area locator does not collapse their boundaries or date modern walls to the Tang.

citations.locator: Successive city locations and later structures

points.label: Luoyang — the house example’s setting
points.text: Bai Juyi’s compound example in the NUS summary belongs to Luoyang. It is not a measured Chang’an house or proof that all wards had that arrangement.
